name: SARS-CoV-2
structure: Enveloped, roughly spherical virion of about 60-140 nm with club-shaped spike (S) glycoprotein trimers, plus membrane (M) and envelope (E) proteins; the helical nucleocapsid (N protein) packages the genome.
genome: Linear, non-segmented, positive-sense single-stranded RNA of about 30 kb, one of the largest RNA virus genomes; encodes its own proofreading exonuclease (nsp14).
transmission: Respiratory droplets and aerosols; less commonly fomites. Spread can occur before symptoms begin.
diseases: COVID-19: from asymptomatic infection to pneumonia and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
Hypercoagulability with venous and arterial thrombosis
Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C)
Post-COVID condition (long COVID)
virulence: Spike receptor-binding domain binds ACE2 on type II pneumocytes and other cells
Host protease TMPRSS2 (and cathepsins) cleave spike to allow membrane fusion
Accessory proteins blunt the type I interferon response
diagnosis: RT-PCR of a nasopharyngeal swab (most sensitive); rapid antigen tests are specific but less sensitive. Imaging may show bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities.
treatment: Supportive care and oxygen. Nirmatrelvir (3CL protease inhibitor, boosted with ritonavir) or remdesivir (RNA polymerase inhibitor) in high-risk patients early; dexamethasone for patients needing oxygen. Watch ritonavir CYP3A4 interactions.
prevention: mRNA and protein-subunit vaccines encoding spike; masking, ventilation and isolation.
pearls: ACE2 receptor, TMPRSS2 priming
Loss of smell and taste is characteristic
Dexamethasone lowers mortality only in patients requiring oxygen
pdb: Spike receptor-binding domain bound to ACE2

name: Influenza A virus
structure: Enveloped, pleomorphic (roughly spherical, about 100 nm) virion studded with hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) spikes; the M2 proton channel spans the envelope and M1 matrix protein lines it.
genome: Negative-sense ssRNA in 8 segments, each packaged as a helical ribonucleoprotein with its own polymerase; segmentation allows reassortment.
transmission: Respiratory droplets, aerosols and fomites; seasonal epidemics in winter.
diseases: Influenza: abrupt fever, myalgia, headache, dry cough
Primary viral pneumonia
Secondary bacterial pneumonia (S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae)
Reye syndrome in children given aspirin
virulence: Hemagglutinin binds sialic acid receptors and mediates membrane fusion
Neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid to release new virions
Antigenic drift (point mutations) causes yearly epidemics; antigenic shift (segment reassortment) causes pandemics
diagnosis: Rapid molecular (NAAT/RT-PCR) testing of a nasopharyngeal swab; rapid antigen tests are less sensitive.
treatment: Neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir, zanamivir, peramivir) or the cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitor baloxavir, ideally within 48 hours of symptom onset. Adamantanes (M2 blockers) are no longer recommended because of widespread resistance.
prevention: Annual inactivated (intramuscular) or live attenuated (intranasal) vaccine, updated for circulating strains.
pearls: Shift = reassortment = pandemic; drift = mutation = epidemic
Post-influenza S. aureus pneumonia
Avoid aspirin in children (Reye syndrome)
pdb: H1 hemagglutinin of influenza A/Puerto Rico/8/1934 (H1N1)

name: Human immunodeficiency virus 1 (HIV-1)
structure: Enveloped virion of about 100-120 nm with gp120/gp41 envelope trimers; a cone-shaped capsid built from p24 protein contains two copies of the genome with reverse transcriptase and integrase.
genome: Diploid, positive-sense ssRNA (about 9.7 kb) with gag (capsid, matrix), pol (reverse transcriptase, integrase, protease) and env (gp120, gp41) plus regulatory genes (tat, rev, nef, vif, vpr, vpu).
transmission: Sexual contact, parenteral (shared needles, transfusion), and vertical (in utero, at delivery, breastfeeding).
diseases: Acute retroviral syndrome (mononucleosis-like illness)
Chronic infection with progressive CD4+ T-cell loss
AIDS: CD4 count below 200/mm3 or an AIDS-defining illness (e.g., Pneumocystis pneumonia, Kaposi sarcoma, toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis, MAC)
virulence: gp120 binds CD4 and a co-receptor (CCR5 early, CXCR4 later); gp41 mediates fusion
Reverse transcriptase is error-prone, driving rapid drug resistance
Integrase inserts proviral DNA into the host genome (latent reservoir)
diagnosis: Fourth-generation HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody combination immunoassay (detects p24 antigen), confirmed with an HIV-1/HIV-2 differentiation assay; HIV RNA viral load for acute infection and monitoring; CD4 count for staging.
treatment: Lifelong antiretroviral therapy, typically an integrase inhibitor (e.g., dolutegravir or bictegravir) plus two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors. Prophylaxis against opportunistic infections according to CD4 count.
prevention: Pre-exposure prophylaxis (tenofovir-based or long-acting cabotegravir), post-exposure prophylaxis, condoms, treatment as prevention (undetectable = untransmittable), and maternal ART to prevent vertical transmission.
pearls: CCR5-delta32 homozygotes are resistant to R5 strains; maraviroc blocks CCR5
Pneumocystis prophylaxis (TMP-SMX) when CD4 < 200
Abacavir: screen HLA-B*57:01 before starting
pdb: HIV-1 protease bound to a cyclic urea inhibitor
Reverse transcriptase with DNA and incoming nucleotide

name: Hepatitis B virus
structure: Enveloped 42 nm Dane particle; envelope carries HBsAg, the icosahedral core is built from HBcAg; infected cells also secrete non-infectious HBsAg spheres and filaments.
genome: Small (about 3.2 kb) circular, partially double-stranded DNA that is replicated through an RNA intermediate by a viral reverse transcriptase; forms persistent cccDNA in hepatocyte nuclei.
transmission: Parenteral, sexual and perinatal; very efficiently transmitted by blood.
diseases: Acute hepatitis (often subclinical; fulminant in a minority)
Chronic hepatitis (about 90% after perinatal infection, under 5% after adult infection)
Cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma
Extrahepatic: polyarteritis nodosa, membranous nephropathy
virulence: Liver damage is mainly immune mediated (cytotoxic T cells)
cccDNA and integrated DNA allow persistence
HBx protein contributes to oncogenesis
diagnosis: Serology: HBsAg (infection), anti-HBs (immunity), IgM anti-HBc (acute infection, positive in the window period), HBeAg and HBV DNA (replication and infectivity).
treatment: Chronic infection: tenofovir or entecavir (nucleos(t)ide analogs) or pegylated interferon-alpha; treat according to ALT, HBV DNA and fibrosis.
prevention: Recombinant HBsAg vaccine (birth dose in infancy); HBIG plus vaccine for exposed newborns and after needle-stick in non-immune people.
pearls: Only anti-HBs positive after vaccination
Window period: IgM anti-HBc is the only positive marker
Hepatitis D needs HBsAg to replicate

name: Hepatitis C virus
structure: Small (about 50 nm) enveloped virion with E1/E2 glycoproteins that circulates bound to lipoproteins.
genome: Positive-sense ssRNA (about 9.6 kb) translated as one polyprotein; the RNA polymerase (NS5B) lacks proofreading, so hypervariable E2 regions evade antibodies.
transmission: Mainly parenteral (injection drug use, historical transfusion, unsafe medical injections); sexual and perinatal transmission are less efficient.
diseases: Acute infection (usually asymptomatic)
Chronic hepatitis in about 70-85%, leading to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma
Extrahepatic: mixed cryoglobulinemia, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, porphyria cutanea tarda, lichen planus
virulence: Lack of proofreading creates quasispecies that escape immunity
No effective vaccine because of antigenic variation
diagnosis: Anti-HCV antibody screening, confirmed by HCV RNA (viral load); genotype as needed.
treatment: Direct-acting antivirals for 8-12 weeks (e.g., sofosbuvir/velpatasvir or glecaprevir/pibrentasvir) cure over 95%. NS5B polymerase inhibitors end in -buvir, NS5A inhibitors in -asvir, NS3/4A protease inhibitors in -previr.
prevention: No vaccine; harm reduction, blood screening and infection control.
pearls: Most common cause of chronic hepatitis needing transplant in many countries before DAAs
Cryoglobulinemia: palpable purpura, arthralgia, low C4

name: Ebola virus
structure: Long filamentous enveloped virion (about 80 nm wide, up to 1,000 nm or more long), often U- or 6-shaped, with a single glycoprotein (GP) spike.
genome: Non-segmented negative-sense ssRNA of about 19 kb encoding 7 genes.
transmission: Direct contact with blood or body fluids of infected people or animals (fruit bats are the presumed reservoir); nosocomial and funeral exposures are important.
diseases: Ebola virus disease: fever, vomiting, diarrhea, then hemorrhage, shock and multiorgan failure; case fatality often 25-90%
virulence: GP mediates entry via the endosomal receptor NPC1
VP35 and VP24 block interferon signaling
Infects macrophages and dendritic cells, causing cytokine storm and DIC
diagnosis: RT-PCR of blood in a high-containment laboratory.
treatment: Aggressive supportive care; monoclonal antibodies against GP (atoltivimab/maftivimab/odesivimab or ansuvimab) for Zaire ebolavirus.
prevention: rVSV-ZEBOV (Ervebo) live recombinant vaccine for ring vaccination; strict infection control with PPE.
pearls: Filamentous shape on electron microscopy
Biosafety level 4 pathogen

name: Measles virus
structure: Pleomorphic enveloped virion (100-300 nm) with hemagglutinin (H) and fusion (F) glycoproteins around a helical nucleocapsid.
genome: Non-segmented negative-sense ssRNA (about 16 kb).
transmission: Airborne; one of the most contagious human infections (R0 about 12-18).
diseases: Measles: cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots, then a maculopapular rash spreading head to toe
Pneumonia (most common cause of measles death) and acute encephalitis
Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis years later
Immune amnesia increases later infections
virulence: H binds SLAM (CD150) on immune cells and nectin-4 on epithelium
F protein causes cell fusion, producing multinucleated Warthin-Finkeldey giant cells
diagnosis: Clinical picture with measles IgM serology or RT-PCR of throat swab or urine.
treatment: Supportive care; vitamin A reduces morbidity and mortality, especially in malnourished children.
prevention: Live attenuated MMR vaccine (two doses); post-exposure vaccine within 72 hours or immune globulin within 6 days.
pearls: Koplik spots: white spots on buccal mucosa before the rash
Vitamin A for all children with measles

name: Poliovirus
structure: Small (about 30 nm), non-enveloped icosahedral capsid made of 60 copies each of VP1-VP4.
genome: Positive-sense ssRNA (about 7.5 kb) with a 5' VPg protein; translated as one polyprotein using an IRES.
transmission: Fecal-oral; replicates in the oropharynx and gut lymphoid tissue (Peyer patches).
diseases: Most infections are asymptomatic or minor illness
Aseptic meningitis
Paralytic poliomyelitis: asymmetric flaccid paralysis from destruction of anterior horn motor neurons
Post-polio syndrome decades later
virulence: Binds CD155 (poliovirus receptor)
Viremia leads to CNS invasion and lower motor neuron destruction
diagnosis: RT-PCR or culture of stool, throat swab or CSF; CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis.
treatment: Supportive; ventilatory support for bulbar involvement.
prevention: Inactivated polio vaccine (IPV, Salk) by injection; oral live attenuated vaccine (OPV, Sabin) gives gut immunity but can rarely revert (vaccine-derived poliovirus).
pearls: Lower motor neuron signs: flaccid paralysis, hyporeflexia, fasciculations, no sensory loss
OPV gives mucosal IgA

name: Rotavirus
structure: Non-enveloped, triple-layered icosahedral capsid (about 75 nm) that looks like a wheel on electron microscopy; outer VP7 and spike VP4.
genome: 11 segments of double-stranded RNA.
transmission: Fecal-oral; very stable in the environment; outbreaks in day care.
diseases: Severe watery diarrhea and vomiting in infants and young children, with dehydration
virulence: NSP4 acts as an enterotoxin and raises intracellular calcium
Villous blunting in the small intestine reduces absorption
diagnosis: Stool antigen test or multiplex PCR.
treatment: Oral rehydration solution; IV fluids for severe dehydration.
prevention: Live oral vaccines (RotaTeq, Rotarix) in infancy; small risk of intussusception.
pearls: Most common cause of severe childhood diarrhea worldwide
Rota = wheel shape
pdb: Atomic model of an infectious rotavirus particle

name: Norovirus
structure: Small non-enveloped icosahedral capsid (about 30-40 nm) built from 180 copies of VP1, with cup-shaped surface depressions.
genome: Positive-sense ssRNA (about 7.5 kb).
transmission: Fecal-oral, vomit aerosols, contaminated food and surfaces; very low infectious dose; outbreaks on cruise ships, nursing homes and schools.
diseases: Acute gastroenteritis with prominent vomiting and watery diarrhea, lasting 1-3 days
virulence: Binds histo-blood group antigens on gut epithelium
Resistant to alcohol hand rubs and many disinfectants
diagnosis: Clinical; stool RT-PCR in outbreaks.
treatment: Oral rehydration and supportive care.
prevention: Hand washing with soap and water, bleach-based cleaning, exclusion of ill food handlers.
pearls: Most common cause of viral gastroenteritis in adults
Alcohol hand rubs are less effective than soap

name: Human papillomavirus
structure: Non-enveloped icosahedral capsid (about 55 nm) made of 72 pentamers of L1 protein with minor protein L2.
genome: Circular double-stranded DNA (about 8 kb).
transmission: Skin-to-skin and sexual contact; perinatal transmission can cause respiratory papillomatosis.
diseases: Common, plantar and flat warts (types 1, 2, 3, 4)
Anogenital warts (condylomata acuminata, types 6 and 11)
Cervical, anal, penile and oropharyngeal cancers (high-risk types 16 and 18, plus others)
Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (types 6 and 11)
virulence: E6 protein promotes degradation of p53
E7 protein inactivates Rb, releasing E2F and driving cell-cycle progression
Integration of viral DNA occurs in many cancers
diagnosis: Cervical cytology (koilocytes) and high-risk HPV DNA testing; biopsy of suspicious lesions.
treatment: Warts: cryotherapy, imiquimod, podophyllotoxin, excision. Precancerous lesions: excision such as LEEP.
prevention: Recombinant L1 virus-like particle vaccine (9-valent), ideally before sexual debut; cervical screening.
pearls: E6 inhibits p53, E7 inhibits Rb
Types 6 and 11 cause warts; 16 and 18 cause cancer

name: Herpes simplex virus 1 and 2
structure: Enveloped virion (about 150-200 nm): icosahedral capsid surrounded by a protein tegument and an envelope derived from the nuclear membrane.
genome: Linear double-stranded DNA (about 152 kb).
transmission: Direct contact with lesions or secretions, including asymptomatic shedding; HSV-2 is mainly sexual; vertical transmission at delivery.
diseases: Gingivostomatitis and herpes labialis (mostly HSV-1)
Genital herpes (mostly HSV-2, increasingly HSV-1)
Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSV-1; temporal lobe)
Keratitis, herpetic whitlow, neonatal herpes, eczema herpeticum
virulence: Latency in sensory ganglia (trigeminal for HSV-1, sacral for HSV-2) with reactivation
Cell-to-cell spread forms multinucleated giant cells
diagnosis: PCR of lesion swab or CSF (encephalitis); Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells (not specific).
treatment: Acyclovir, valacyclovir or famciclovir (need viral thymidine kinase); IV acyclovir for encephalitis and neonatal disease; foscarnet for acyclovir-resistant strains.
prevention: Suppressive antivirals reduce transmission; cesarean delivery when genital lesions are present at labor.
pearls: Temporal lobe encephalitis: start IV acyclovir immediately
Acyclovir resistance via thymidine kinase mutation: use foscarnet

name: Varicella-zoster virus
structure: Enveloped herpesvirus with icosahedral capsid and tegument.
genome: Linear double-stranded DNA (about 125 kb), the smallest human herpesvirus genome.
transmission: Airborne and contact with vesicle fluid; highly contagious.
diseases: Varicella (chickenpox): crops of pruritic vesicles at different stages, centripetal distribution
Herpes zoster (shingles): painful dermatomal vesicular rash from reactivation
Postherpetic neuralgia, herpes zoster ophthalmicus, Ramsay Hunt syndrome
Varicella pneumonia in adults and pregnancy; congenital varicella syndrome
virulence: Latency in dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia
diagnosis: Clinical; PCR of vesicle fluid when needed.
treatment: Acyclovir or valacyclovir (zoster within 72 hours; varicella in adults and high-risk children).
prevention: Live attenuated varicella vaccine; recombinant adjuvanted zoster vaccine (Shingrix) for adults 50 and older; VariZIG for exposed high-risk people.
pearls: Lesions in different stages at the same time (unlike smallpox)
Zoster ophthalmicus: tip-of-nose lesion (Hutchinson sign)

name: Epstein-Barr virus
structure: Enveloped herpesvirus; glycoprotein gp350 binds CD21 on B cells.
genome: Linear double-stranded DNA (about 172 kb) that persists as an episome in latently infected B cells.
transmission: Saliva (kissing disease); less often transfusion and transplantation.
diseases: Infectious mononucleosis: fever, exudative pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly
Burkitt lymphoma (endemic African), Hodgkin lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma
Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder, primary CNS lymphoma in HIV
Oral hairy leukoplakia in HIV
virulence: Infects B cells via CD21 (complement receptor 2)
Latent proteins (EBNA, LMP-1) immortalize B cells
diagnosis: Heterophile antibody (Monospot) test; EBV-specific antibodies (VCA IgM) when Monospot is negative; atypical lymphocytes (reactive CD8+ T cells) on smear.
treatment: Supportive; avoid contact sports for at least 3-4 weeks (splenic rupture risk).
prevention: No vaccine.
pearls: Amoxicillin in mononucleosis causes a maculopapular rash
CD21 receptor; atypical cells are CD8+ T cells

name: Cytomegalovirus
structure: Enveloped herpesvirus; infected cells enlarge with intranuclear 'owl's eye' inclusions.
genome: Linear double-stranded DNA (about 235 kb), the largest human herpesvirus genome.
transmission: Saliva, urine, sexual contact, transplacental, breast milk, transfusion and organ transplantation.
diseases: Mononucleosis-like illness (heterophile negative)
Congenital CMV: most common congenital infection; sensorineural hearing loss, periventricular calcifications, microcephaly
In immunocompromised: retinitis (CD4 < 50), colitis, esophagitis, pneumonitis (transplant)
virulence: Latency in monocytes and other myeloid cells
diagnosis: PCR (blood, urine, saliva in newborns); histology shows owl's eye inclusions.
treatment: Ganciclovir or valganciclovir (phosphorylated by viral UL97 kinase); foscarnet or cidofovir for resistance; letermovir for prophylaxis in transplant recipients.
prevention: CMV-negative or leukoreduced blood for at-risk recipients; prophylaxis or pre-emptive therapy after transplant.
pearls: Periventricular calcifications (toxoplasmosis: diffuse)
Ganciclovir causes myelosuppression; foscarnet causes nephrotoxicity and electrolyte loss

name: Dengue virus
structure: Enveloped virion (about 50 nm) with icosahedral arrangement of envelope (E) protein dimers lying flat on the surface.
genome: Positive-sense ssRNA (about 11 kb); four serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4).
transmission: Bite of Aedes aegypti (and Aedes albopictus) mosquitoes.
diseases: Dengue fever: high fever, retro-orbital headache, severe myalgia and arthralgia (breakbone fever), rash
Severe dengue with plasma leakage, bleeding and shock, especially with a second, different serotype
virulence: Antibody-dependent enhancement: non-neutralizing antibodies from a prior serotype increase infection of Fc receptor-bearing cells
diagnosis: NS1 antigen or RT-PCR in the first week; IgM serology afterwards. Positive tourniquet test, thrombocytopenia and rising hematocrit are warning signs.
treatment: Supportive with careful fluid management; acetaminophen for fever. Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs (bleeding risk).
prevention: Mosquito control; vaccines (e.g., TAK-003, or CYD-TDV only for people with prior infection).
pearls: Second infection with a different serotype has the highest risk of severe dengue
Avoid NSAIDs

name: Zika virus
structure: Enveloped icosahedral flavivirus (about 50 nm) with E and M proteins on the surface.
genome: Positive-sense ssRNA (about 10.8 kb).
transmission: Aedes mosquito bite; also sexual, transplacental and transfusion.
diseases: Usually mild: rash, fever, conjunctivitis, arthralgia
Congenital Zika syndrome: microcephaly, ocular defects, contractures
Guillain-Barre syndrome
virulence: Infects neural progenitor cells in the developing brain
diagnosis: RT-PCR of serum or urine; IgM serology (cross-reacts with dengue).
treatment: Supportive.
prevention: Mosquito avoidance; pregnant people avoid travel to active areas; condoms.
pearls: Congenital microcephaly
Serologic cross-reactivity with dengue
pdb: Cryo-EM structure of mature Zika virus

name: Rabies virus
structure: Bullet-shaped enveloped virion (about 75 x 180 nm) with glycoprotein G spikes and a helical nucleocapsid.
genome: Non-segmented negative-sense ssRNA (about 12 kb).
transmission: Bite or scratch of an infected animal (dogs worldwide; bats, raccoons, skunks, foxes in the Americas).
diseases: Rabies encephalitis: prodrome with paresthesia at the bite site, then furious (agitation, hydrophobia, hypersalivation) or paralytic form; almost always fatal once symptomatic
virulence: G protein binds the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction
Travels by retrograde axonal transport (dynein) to the CNS
Negri bodies: cytoplasmic inclusions in Purkinje cells and hippocampal neurons
diagnosis: Antemortem: RT-PCR of saliva, skin biopsy from the nape of the neck (antigen), and serum/CSF antibodies.
treatment: No effective treatment after symptoms appear; prevention is essential.
prevention: Post-exposure prophylaxis: wound washing, human rabies immune globulin infiltrated at the wound, and inactivated vaccine (days 0, 3, 7, 14); pre-exposure vaccine for high-risk groups.
pearls: Long incubation allows post-exposure prophylaxis to work
Bites closer to the CNS have shorter incubation

name: Human adenovirus
structure: Non-enveloped icosahedral capsid (about 90 nm) built from hexons and pentons, with a fiber protruding from each of the 12 vertices.
genome: Linear double-stranded DNA (about 26-45 kb).
transmission: Respiratory droplets, fecal-oral, direct eye contact (swimming pools, contaminated instruments).
diseases: Pharyngitis and pharyngoconjunctival fever
Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis
Acute hemorrhagic cystitis
Gastroenteritis in children (types 40 and 41); pneumonia in military recruits and immunocompromised hosts
virulence: Fiber protein binds the coxsackie-adenovirus receptor (CAR)
Non-enveloped, so resistant to drying and many disinfectants
diagnosis: PCR or antigen testing of the relevant sample.
treatment: Supportive; cidofovir for severe disease in immunocompromised patients.
prevention: Oral live vaccine (types 4 and 7) for military recruits; hand hygiene and instrument disinfection.
pearls: Hemorrhagic cystitis after hematopoietic stem cell transplant (also BK virus)
Conjunctivitis plus pharyngitis plus fever

name: Respiratory syncytial virus
structure: Enveloped, pleomorphic or filamentous virion with attachment (G) and fusion (F) glycoproteins; no hemagglutinin or neuraminidase.
genome: Non-segmented negative-sense ssRNA (about 15 kb).
transmission: Respiratory droplets and contaminated hands and surfaces; winter epidemics.
diseases: Bronchiolitis in infants (wheeze, crackles, hypoxia)
Pneumonia in infants and older adults
virulence: F protein fuses infected cells into syncytia
Infection of small airway epithelium causes mucus plugging and air trapping
diagnosis: Clinical in infants; rapid antigen or PCR of nasopharyngeal swab.
treatment: Supportive: oxygen, suction, hydration. Ribavirin only in selected severely immunocompromised patients.
prevention: Nirsevimab or palivizumab (monoclonal antibodies against F) for infants; maternal RSV vaccine; vaccines for older adults.
pearls: Most common cause of bronchiolitis and infant pneumonia
Monoclonal antibodies target the F protein
pdb: Prefusion F glycoprotein bound to an antibody

name: Bacteriophage T4
structure: Elongated icosahedral head (about 85 x 115 nm), a contractile tail sheath and six long tail fibers that attach to E. coli.
genome: Linear double-stranded DNA (about 169 kb).
transmission: Infects Escherichia coli; does not infect humans.
diseases: Not a human pathogen; model organism for molecular biology
virulence: Tail contraction injects DNA through the bacterial envelope

Relevance to medicine: phage therapy and transduction, the mechanism by which phages transfer bacterial genes such as toxin genes (e.g., diphtheria, cholera, Shiga, botulinum toxins are phage encoded or lysogenic conversion)
diagnosis: Not applicable.
treatment: Not applicable.
prevention: Not applicable.
pearls: Lysogenic conversion genes (ABCDE): shigA-like toxin, botulinum toxin, cholera toxin, diphtheria toxin, erythrogenic toxin of S. pyogenes

name: Staphylococcus aureus
structure: Gram-positive cocci in grape-like clusters; catalase positive, coagulase positive, beta-hemolytic, forms golden colonies; ferments mannitol.
genome: Circular chromosome (about 2.8 Mb) plus plasmids and mobile elements (SCCmec carries mecA in MRSA).
transmission: Colonizes anterior nares and skin; spreads by hands, contact and fomites.
diseases: Skin and soft tissue: impetigo, folliculitis, abscess, cellulitis
Invasive: bacteremia, acute endocarditis (tricuspid valve in injection drug use), osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, post-influenza pneumonia
Toxin-mediated: toxic shock syndrome (TSST-1), scalded skin syndrome (exfoliative toxin), food poisoning (preformed enterotoxin, onset 2-6 hours)
virulence: Protein A binds the Fc region of IgG, preventing opsonization
Coagulase forms a fibrin coat
TSST-1 is a superantigen that cross-links MHC II and the T-cell receptor
Panton-Valentine leukocidin in community MRSA; altered PBP2a (mecA) gives methicillin resistance
diagnosis: Gram stain and culture; catalase and coagulase tests; PCR for mecA.
treatment: MSSA: nafcillin, oxacillin or cefazolin. MRSA: vancomycin, daptomycin (not for pneumonia) or linezolid; for uncomplicated skin infections TMP-SMX, doxycycline or clindamycin. Drain abscesses.
prevention: Hand hygiene, contact precautions, decolonization (mupirocin, chlorhexidine) in selected settings.
pearls: Most common cause of osteomyelitis overall and of acute bacterial endocarditis
Food poisoning is due to preformed heat-stable toxin, so it starts quickly

name: Streptococcus pyogenes (group A strep)
structure: Gram-positive cocci in chains; catalase negative, beta-hemolytic, bacitracin sensitive, PYR positive; hyaluronic acid capsule.
genome: Circular chromosome (about 1.9 Mb) with prophages that carry toxin genes.
transmission: Respiratory droplets and skin contact.
diseases: Pyogenic: pharyngitis, impetigo, cellulitis, erysipelas, necrotizing fasciitis
Toxigenic: scarlet fever, streptococcal toxic shock syndrome
Immunologic: acute rheumatic fever (after pharyngitis only), post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (after pharyngitis or skin infection)
virulence: M protein is antiphagocytic and its molecular mimicry with cardiac myosin causes rheumatic fever
Streptolysin O (antigenic, ASO titer) and streptolysin S
Streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins (erythrogenic toxin) are superantigens
Streptokinase and hyaluronidase help spread
diagnosis: Rapid antigen test or culture of throat swab; ASO and anti-DNase B titers for post-streptococcal disease; Centor criteria guide testing.
treatment: Penicillin V or amoxicillin; cephalexin or azithromycin/clindamycin if allergic. Necrotizing fasciitis: surgical debridement plus penicillin and clindamycin (clindamycin suppresses toxin production).
prevention: Treating pharyngitis prevents rheumatic fever (but not glomerulonephritis); secondary prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin after rheumatic fever.
pearls: PHaRM: Pyrogenic toxin, Hyaluronic capsule, Rheumatic fever, M protein
Rheumatic fever: Jones criteria (J-O-N-E-S)

name: Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus)
structure: Encapsulated gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci; alpha-hemolytic, optochin sensitive, bile soluble; positive Quellung reaction.
genome: Circular chromosome (about 2.1 Mb); naturally competent for transformation.
transmission: Respiratory droplets; colonizes the nasopharynx.
diseases: Most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia (lobar, rust-colored sputum)
Meningitis in adults and older children
Otitis media and sinusitis
Bacteremia, especially after splenectomy or in sickle cell disease
virulence: Polysaccharide capsule is the main virulence factor (antiphagocytic)
IgA protease
Pneumolysin damages cells and activates complement
diagnosis: Gram stain and culture of sputum, blood or CSF; urinary antigen test.
treatment: Community-acquired pneumonia: beta-lactam (amoxicillin, ceftriaxone) with or without a macrolide, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone. Meningitis: ceftriaxone plus vancomycin plus dexamethasone until susceptibility is known.
prevention: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCV15, PCV20, PCV21) and polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23).
pearls: MOPS: Meningitis, Otitis media, Pneumonia, Sinusitis
Asplenia predisposes to encapsulated organisms

name: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
structure: Slender, slow-growing obligate aerobic rod with a waxy mycolic acid-rich cell wall that resists Gram staining but is acid fast (Ziehl-Neelsen).
genome: Circular chromosome (about 4.4 Mb).
transmission: Airborne droplet nuclei from people with active pulmonary disease.
diseases: Primary TB: Ghon focus in the lower or middle lobes plus hilar nodes (Ghon complex)
Latent TB infection
Secondary (reactivation) TB: cavitary apical upper-lobe disease with fever, night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis
Extrapulmonary: miliary TB, TB meningitis, Pott disease (spine), adrenal and renal TB
virulence: Cord factor (trehalose dimycolate) activates macrophages and promotes granuloma formation
Sulfatides inhibit phagolysosome fusion
Survives inside macrophages; caseating granulomas
diagnosis: Latent: tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay. Active: chest radiograph, sputum acid-fast smear, culture and nucleic acid amplification (e.g., Xpert MTB/RIF, which also detects rifampin resistance).
treatment: Active disease: rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 2 months, then rifampin and isoniazid for 4 months (RIPE). Give pyridoxine with isoniazid. Latent: rifampin-based or isoniazid-rifapentine regimens.
prevention: BCG vaccine (protects children from severe disease); treatment of latent infection; airborne isolation.
pearls: Isoniazid: peripheral neuropathy (give B6), hepatotoxicity; rifampin: orange body fluids, CYP inducer; ethambutol: optic neuritis; pyrazinamide: hyperuricemia
IGRA is not affected by prior BCG

name: Escherichia coli
structure: Gram-negative, facultatively anaerobic rod with peritrichous flagella, fimbriae and lipopolysaccharide (O antigen); ferments lactose (pink on MacConkey), green metallic sheen on EMB agar.
genome: Circular chromosome (about 4.6 Mb) plus plasmids; pathotypes acquire virulence genes on plasmids, phages and pathogenicity islands.
transmission: Endogenous gut flora (urinary tract infections); fecal-oral and contaminated food for diarrheal strains (e.g., undercooked beef for O157:H7).
diseases: Urinary tract infection and pyelonephritis (most common cause)
Neonatal meningitis (K1 capsule) and sepsis
Traveler's diarrhea (ETEC), bloody diarrhea and hemolytic uremic syndrome (EHEC O157:H7)
Intra-abdominal infection, nosocomial pneumonia
virulence: P fimbriae (pyelonephritis) and type 1 fimbriae (cystitis)
K1 capsule (neonatal meningitis)
LPS endotoxin (septic shock)
Shiga-like toxin inactivates the 60S ribosome (EHEC); heat-labile and heat-stable toxins (ETEC)
diagnosis: Culture with susceptibility testing; urinalysis (positive nitrite, leukocyte esterase); EHEC: sorbitol MacConkey (O157:H7 does not ferment sorbitol) and Shiga toxin assay.
treatment: Guided by susceptibility (rising ESBL resistance). Cystitis: nitrofurantoin, TMP-SMX or fosfomycin. Avoid antibiotics in EHEC diarrhea (may increase HUS risk).
prevention: Food safety, hand hygiene, catheter care.
pearls: EHEC O157:H7 does not ferment sorbitol and does not produce glucuronidase
HUS: anemia, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury

name: Vibrio cholerae
structure: Curved (comma-shaped) gram-negative rod with a single polar flagellum; oxidase positive; grows on alkaline media (TCBS agar, yellow colonies).
genome: Two circular chromosomes; the cholera toxin genes are carried by the CTX-phi bacteriophage.
transmission: Fecal-contaminated water and seafood; high infectious dose because the organism is acid sensitive.
diseases: Cholera: profuse 'rice-water' diarrhea leading to hypovolemic shock
virulence: Cholera toxin (A-B toxin) ADP-ribosylates Gs alpha, permanently activating adenylate cyclase; high cAMP drives chloride secretion through CFTR
Toxin-coregulated pilus for colonization
diagnosis: Stool culture on TCBS agar; rapid antigen tests in outbreaks.
treatment: Prompt oral rehydration solution (or IV fluids in severe cases) is life saving; antibiotics (doxycycline or azithromycin) shorten illness.
prevention: Safe water and sanitation; oral cholera vaccines.
pearls: Cholera toxin turns Gs 'on'; pertussis toxin turns Gi 'off' (both raise cAMP)
Rehydration is the key treatment

name: Clostridioides difficile
structure: Obligately anaerobic, spore-forming gram-positive rod; spores resist alcohol and many disinfectants.
genome: Circular chromosome (about 4.3 Mb) with the pathogenicity locus encoding toxins A and B.
transmission: Fecal-oral spread of spores, especially in hospitals and long-term care; disease follows disruption of the gut microbiota by antibiotics (clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins, amoxicillin).
diseases: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea
Pseudomembranous colitis
Fulminant colitis with toxic megacolon
virulence: Toxin A (enterotoxin) and toxin B (cytotoxin) glucosylate Rho GTPases, disrupting the actin cytoskeleton
Hypervirulent strains (e.g., NAP1/027) produce more toxin and binary toxin
diagnosis: Stool PCR for toxin genes and/or enzyme immunoassay for toxins, in patients with 3 or more unformed stools in 24 hours.
treatment: Oral fidaxomicin or oral vancomycin; for fulminant disease oral vancomycin plus IV metronidazole and surgical evaluation; fecal microbiota transplantation for recurrent disease; bezlotoxumab (anti-toxin B) to reduce recurrence.
prevention: Antibiotic stewardship; contact precautions; soap-and-water hand washing (alcohol does not kill spores); bleach cleaning.
pearls: Oral vancomycin, not IV, for C. difficile
Alcohol hand rub does not kill spores

name: Clostridium tetani
structure: Anaerobic gram-positive rod with a terminal spore that gives a 'tennis racket' or drumstick appearance.
genome: Chromosome plus a plasmid that encodes tetanospasmin.
transmission: Spores in soil enter through contaminated wounds (puncture wounds, burns, umbilical stump in neonates).
diseases: Tetanus: trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus, opisthotonus, generalized spastic paralysis and autonomic instability
Neonatal tetanus
virulence: Tetanospasmin travels retrogradely to the spinal cord and cleaves synaptobrevin, blocking release of GABA and glycine from Renshaw cells
diagnosis: Clinical.
treatment: Human tetanus immune globulin, wound debridement, metronidazole, benzodiazepines for spasms, airway support; give tetanus vaccine (disease does not confer immunity).
prevention: Tetanus toxoid vaccine (DTaP, Tdap, Td boosters); wound management with toxoid with or without immune globulin.
pearls: Tetanus toxin blocks inhibitory neurotransmitters (spastic paralysis); botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine (flaccid paralysis)

name: Clostridium botulinum
structure: Anaerobic, spore-forming gram-positive rod.
genome: Botulinum neurotoxin genes may be chromosomal, plasmid or phage encoded depending on toxin type.
transmission: Foodborne (preformed toxin in improperly canned or preserved foods), infant botulism (ingested spores, e.g., honey), wound botulism (injection drug use).
diseases: Botulism: symmetric descending flaccid paralysis beginning with cranial nerves (diplopia, ptosis, dysphagia, dysarthria), without fever or sensory loss
Infant botulism: constipation, poor feeding, floppy baby
virulence: Botulinum toxin is a zinc protease that cleaves SNARE proteins (SNAP-25, synaptobrevin or syntaxin depending on the toxin type), blocking acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction
diagnosis: Clinical; toxin detection in serum, stool or food (public health laboratory).
treatment: Botulinum antitoxin as early as possible (heptavalent for adults; BabyBIG for infants) plus respiratory support.
prevention: Proper canning; no honey for infants under 12 months.
pearls: Descending paralysis (Guillain-Barre is ascending)
Therapeutic use: dystonia, spasticity, migraine, hyperhidrosis, cosmetic

name: Corynebacterium diphtheriae
structure: Club-shaped gram-positive rods arranged like Chinese characters, with metachromatic (Babes-Ernst) granules.
genome: Diphtheria toxin gene (tox) is carried by beta-prophage (lysogenic conversion).
transmission: Respiratory droplets; cutaneous contact.
diseases: Diphtheria: pharyngitis with an adherent grey pseudomembrane, 'bull neck' lymphadenopathy
Myocarditis with arrhythmia and cranial or peripheral neuropathy from toxin
virulence: Diphtheria toxin (A-B toxin) ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2, stopping protein synthesis
diagnosis: Culture on cysteine-tellurite (black colonies) or Loeffler medium; Elek test for toxin production.
treatment: Diphtheria antitoxin plus penicillin or erythromycin; vaccinate close contacts.
prevention: Diphtheria toxoid vaccine (DTaP, Tdap).
pearls: ABCDEFG: ADP-ribosylation, Beta-prophage, Corynebacterium, Diphtheriae, Elongation Factor 2, Granules

name: Bacillus anthracis
structure: Large gram-positive rods in chains ('boxcar' appearance) with a unique polypeptide (poly-D-glutamate) capsule; spore former.
genome: Chromosome plus plasmids pXO1 (toxin genes) and pXO2 (capsule genes).
transmission: Contact with spores from animals or animal products (wool, hides), inhalation, ingestion; bioterrorism agent.
diseases: Cutaneous anthrax: painless papule that becomes an ulcer with a black eschar and surrounding edema
Inhalational anthrax (woolsorters' disease): flu-like illness then hemorrhagic mediastinitis (widened mediastinum) and shock
Gastrointestinal anthrax
virulence: Protective antigen forms a pore that delivers edema factor (adenylate cyclase) and lethal factor (protease that cleaves MAP kinase kinases)
Poly-D-glutamate capsule is antiphagocytic
diagnosis: Gram stain and culture; PCR; chest CT showing mediastinal widening in inhalational disease.
treatment: Ciprofloxacin or doxycycline; combination therapy and anthrax antitoxins (raxibacumab, obiltoxaximab) for systemic disease.
prevention: Anthrax vaccine adsorbed for high-risk workers; post-exposure antibiotics plus vaccine.
pearls: Only bacterium with a polypeptide (protein) capsule
Edema factor mimics adenylate cyclase

name: Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus)
structure: Encapsulated gram-negative kidney-bean-shaped diplococci; oxidase positive; ferments maltose and glucose.
genome: Circular chromosome (about 2.2 Mb); naturally transformable.
transmission: Respiratory droplets; outbreaks in dormitories, military barracks and the African meningitis belt.
diseases: Meningitis (fever, neck stiffness, petechial or purpuric rash)
Meningococcemia with disseminated intravascular coagulation
Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (adrenal hemorrhage)
virulence: Polysaccharide capsule
Lipooligosaccharide (LOS) endotoxin drives shock and DIC
IgA protease; pili
diagnosis: Gram stain, culture and PCR of CSF or blood; grows on chocolate or Thayer-Martin agar.
treatment: Ceftriaxone or penicillin G. Close contacts receive prophylaxis (rifampin, ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone).
prevention: Conjugate vaccines (MenACWY) and MenB vaccines; recommended for adolescents, asplenia, complement deficiency and eculizumab therapy.
pearls: Terminal complement (C5-C9) deficiency causes recurrent Neisseria infections
Eculizumab blocks C5: vaccinate first

name: Neisseria gonorrhoeae (gonococcus)
structure: Gram-negative diplococci, often inside neutrophils; no polysaccharide capsule; ferments glucose only.
genome: Circular chromosome; antigenic variation of pili and Opa proteins.
transmission: Sexual and perinatal.
diseases: Urethritis, cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease (infertility, ectopic pregnancy), epididymitis
Disseminated gonococcal infection: tenosynovitis, dermatitis and migratory polyarthritis or purulent septic arthritis
Neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum, days 2-5)
Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis)
virulence: Pili with antigenic variation prevent lasting immunity
IgA protease; lipooligosaccharide
diagnosis: Nucleic acid amplification testing of urine or genital, rectal or pharyngeal swabs; culture on Thayer-Martin agar for susceptibility.
treatment: Ceftriaxone single intramuscular dose; add doxycycline if chlamydia has not been excluded. Treat partners.
prevention: Condoms; erythromycin eye ointment at birth.
pearls: No vaccine because of antigenic variation
Septic arthritis in a sexually active young adult: think gonococcus

name: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
structure: Aerobic gram-negative rod; oxidase positive, non-lactose fermenting; produces blue-green pigments (pyocyanin, pyoverdine) and a grape-like odor.
genome: Large chromosome (about 6.3 Mb) with many efflux pumps and resistance genes.
transmission: Water and moist environments (hot tubs, sinks, ventilators, contact lens solution); nosocomial spread.
diseases: Hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia; chronic infection in cystic fibrosis (mucoid strains)
Burn wound infection, otitis externa (swimmer's ear) and malignant otitis externa in diabetes
Hot tub folliculitis, ecthyma gangrenosum, keratitis in contact lens wearers
UTI with catheters; osteomyelitis after puncture through a shoe
virulence: Exotoxin A inactivates EF-2 (like diphtheria toxin)
Alginate biofilm (mucoid strains in CF)
Phospholipase C, elastase, type III secretion system
diagnosis: Culture (non-lactose fermenting, oxidase-positive colonies with green pigment).
treatment: Antipseudomonal agents guided by susceptibility: piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime or ceftazidime, carbapenems (not ertapenem), fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin), aminoglycosides; ceftolozane-tazobactam for resistant strains.
prevention: Infection control and water management in hospitals.
pearls: Ertapenem lacks Pseudomonas activity
Malignant otitis externa in elderly diabetic patients

name: Helicobacter pylori
structure: Curved or spiral gram-negative rod with multiple flagella; microaerophilic; catalase, oxidase and urease positive.
genome: Circular chromosome (about 1.7 Mb); cag pathogenicity island in more virulent strains.
transmission: Probably fecal-oral or oral-oral; acquired mainly in childhood.
diseases: Chronic gastritis (antral)
Duodenal and gastric peptic ulcers
Gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma
virulence: Urease produces ammonia that neutralizes acid around the organism
CagA (injected by a type IV secretion system) and VacA (vacuolating cytotoxin)
diagnosis: Urea breath test or stool antigen (non-invasive, confirm eradication); biopsy with rapid urease test or histology during endoscopy. Stop PPIs 2 weeks before testing when possible.
treatment: Bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI, bismuth, tetracycline, metronidazole) or other combinations such as PPI with amoxicillin and rifabutin, chosen by local clarithromycin resistance; confirm eradication.
prevention: No vaccine.
pearls: Most duodenal ulcers are associated with H. pylori
Eradication can regress early MALT lymphoma

name: Treponema pallidum
structure: Thin, tightly coiled spirochete with endoflagella (axial filaments); too thin to see on Gram stain; seen by dark-field microscopy or fluorescent antibody.
genome: Small circular chromosome (about 1.1 Mb); cannot be cultured on artificial media.
transmission: Sexual contact, transplacental.
diseases: Primary syphilis: painless indurated chancre
Secondary: diffuse maculopapular rash including palms and soles, condylomata lata, lymphadenopathy
Tertiary: gummas, aortitis (ascending aorta aneurysm), neurosyphilis (tabes dorsalis, general paresis, Argyll Robertson pupil)
Congenital syphilis: saddle nose, Hutchinson teeth, saber shins, sensorineural deafness
virulence: Few surface proteins, allowing immune evasion
Endarteritis obliterans
diagnosis: Non-treponemal tests (RPR, VDRL; titers follow treatment) and treponemal tests (FTA-ABS, TP-PA, EIA; stay positive); dark-field microscopy of chancre; CSF VDRL for neurosyphilis.
treatment: Benzathine penicillin G intramuscularly (one dose for early syphilis, three weekly doses for late latent); IV aqueous penicillin G for neurosyphilis; desensitize pregnant patients who are allergic.
prevention: Screening in pregnancy; condoms; partner treatment.
pearls: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction: fever and myalgia hours after treatment from released lipoproteins
False-positive VDRL: pregnancy, viral infection, lupus and antiphospholipid antibodies

name: Chlamydia trachomatis
structure: Obligate intracellular gram-negative-like bacterium without muramic acid in its cell wall; infectious elementary body and replicating reticulate body (intracytoplasmic inclusions).
genome: Small circular chromosome (about 1 Mb) and a plasmid.
transmission: Sexual, perinatal, and eye-to-eye contact by flies and hands for trachoma.
diseases: Serovars A-C: trachoma (leading infectious cause of blindness)
Serovars D-K: urethritis, cervicitis, PID, epididymitis, reactive arthritis, neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia (staccato cough)
Serovars L1-L3: lymphogranuloma venereum
virulence: Intracellular life cycle avoids host defenses
Inflammatory scarring causes infertility and ectopic pregnancy
diagnosis: Nucleic acid amplification test of urine or genital swab; cytoplasmic inclusions on Giemsa stain.
treatment: Doxycycline for 7 days (azithromycin single dose in pregnancy); treat partners.
prevention: Annual screening of sexually active women under 25 and others at risk; condoms.
pearls: Most common bacterial sexually transmitted infection
Reactive arthritis: urethritis, conjunctivitis, arthritis

name: Listeria monocytogenes
structure: Facultative intracellular gram-positive rod; tumbling motility at room temperature; beta-hemolytic; grows at refrigerator temperature (cold enrichment).
genome: Circular chromosome (about 2.9 Mb).
transmission: Contaminated foods (unpasteurized dairy, soft cheeses, deli meats, refrigerated ready-to-eat foods), transplacental and at delivery.
diseases: Meningitis in neonates, older adults and immunocompromised patients
Amnionitis, sepsis and spontaneous abortion in pregnancy; granulomatosis infantiseptica
Febrile gastroenteritis in healthy people
virulence: Listeriolysin O lets the organism escape the phagosome
ActA polymerizes host actin ('rocket tails') for cell-to-cell spread
diagnosis: Culture of blood or CSF.
treatment: Ampicillin (plus gentamicin in severe disease); TMP-SMX if penicillin allergic. Cephalosporins are not active.
prevention: Pregnant and immunocompromised people avoid unpasteurized dairy and deli meats.
pearls: Add ampicillin to empiric meningitis therapy in neonates and adults over 50
Actin rocket tails

name: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi
structure: Motile gram-negative rod with a Vi capsule; non-lactose fermenting, produces hydrogen sulfide on triple sugar iron agar.
genome: Circular chromosome with Salmonella pathogenicity islands (type III secretion systems).
transmission: Fecal-oral through contaminated water and food; humans are the only reservoir (chronic carriers in the gallbladder).
diseases: Typhoid (enteric) fever: stepwise fever, relative bradycardia, abdominal pain, rose spots, constipation then diarrhea, hepatosplenomegaly
Complications: intestinal hemorrhage and perforation (Peyer patches)
Chronic carrier state
virulence: Vi capsule
Survives inside macrophages; spreads through the reticuloendothelial system
diagnosis: Blood culture (first week), bone marrow culture is most sensitive; stool culture later.
treatment: Ceftriaxone or azithromycin; fluoroquinolones only if susceptible (widespread resistance, extensively drug-resistant strains in Pakistan respond to carbapenems or azithromycin).
prevention: Typhoid conjugate vaccine, Vi polysaccharide vaccine or oral live Ty21a; safe water and sanitation.
pearls: Rose spots on the abdomen
Extensively drug-resistant typhoid emerged in Sindh, Pakistan, in 2016

name: Candida albicans
structure: Oval budding yeast that forms pseudohyphae and true hyphae at body temperature; germ tube positive at 37 C.
genome: Diploid nuclear genome (about 14 Mb per haploid set).
transmission: Endogenous normal flora of mouth, gut and vagina; disease follows antibiotics, immunosuppression, diabetes, catheters.
diseases: Oral thrush, esophagitis (HIV), vulvovaginitis, intertrigo, diaper dermatitis
Candidemia and disseminated candidiasis (central lines, neutropenia, TPN)
Endocarditis in injection drug use; chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis with T-cell defects
virulence: Hyphal invasion and adhesins
Biofilm on catheters
diagnosis: KOH preparation showing budding yeast and pseudohyphae; culture; beta-D-glucan for invasive disease.
treatment: Topical azoles or nystatin for superficial infection; oral fluconazole for esophagitis and vaginitis; an echinocandin (caspofungin, micafungin) for candidemia, remove central lines; amphotericin B for some severe infections.
prevention: Line care; fluconazole prophylaxis in selected high-risk patients.
pearls: Thrush in an adult without risk factors: test for HIV
Germ tube test identifies C. albicans

name: Aspergillus fumigatus
structure: Mold with septate hyphae that branch at acute (45 degree) angles; conidia are inhaled.
genome: Haploid genome of about 29 Mb.
transmission: Inhalation of airborne conidia from soil, compost and construction dust; not person to person.
diseases: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (asthma, cystic fibrosis)
Aspergilloma (fungus ball) in pre-existing cavities (e.g., after TB)
Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis
Invasive aspergillosis in neutropenia or transplant (halo sign on CT)
virulence: Angioinvasion causes infarction and hemorrhage
Aflatoxins (A. flavus) cause hepatocellular carcinoma
diagnosis: Imaging, galactomannan antigen, culture and histology; ABPA: high IgE, eosinophilia, positive Aspergillus skin test or specific IgE.
treatment: Invasive: voriconazole (or isavuconazole); ABPA: corticosteroids with itraconazole; aspergilloma: surgery when symptomatic.
prevention: HEPA filtration and posaconazole prophylaxis for high-risk patients.
pearls: Acute-angle septate hyphae (Mucor: wide, non-septate, right-angle hyphae)
Voriconazole: visual disturbances, photosensitivity, hepatotoxicity

name: Cryptococcus neoformans
structure: Round yeast with a thick polysaccharide capsule (clear halo on India ink); narrow-based budding; urease positive.
genome: Haploid genome of about 19 Mb.
transmission: Inhalation of yeast from soil contaminated with pigeon droppings.
diseases: Cryptococcal meningitis in advanced HIV (CD4 < 100) and other immunocompromised hosts, with raised intracranial pressure
Pneumonia
virulence: Polysaccharide capsule is antiphagocytic
Melanin production
diagnosis: Cryptococcal antigen in serum or CSF (latex agglutination or lateral flow); India ink stain; culture; very high CSF opening pressure.
treatment: Induction with amphotericin B plus flucytosine, then fluconazole consolidation and maintenance; therapeutic lumbar punctures for raised pressure; delay ART start by several weeks to reduce IRIS risk.
prevention: Cryptococcal antigen screening and pre-emptive fluconazole in advanced HIV.
pearls: Soap bubble lesions in the basal ganglia on MRI
India ink halo

name: Pneumocystis jirovecii
structure: Yeast-like fungus that cannot be cultured; cysts appear as 'crushed ping-pong balls' on methenamine silver stain; cell membrane lacks ergosterol.
genome: Small haploid genome (about 8 Mb).
transmission: Inhalation; person-to-person airborne spread.
diseases: Pneumocystis pneumonia in HIV (CD4 < 200), transplant recipients and patients on long-term corticosteroids: dry cough, dyspnea, hypoxia, bilateral diffuse interstitial infiltrates
virulence: Attaches to type I pneumocytes, filling alveoli with foamy exudate
diagnosis: Bronchoalveolar lavage or induced sputum with silver or immunofluorescent stain, or PCR; elevated LDH and beta-D-glucan; CT shows ground-glass opacities.
treatment: TMP-SMX; add corticosteroids if PaO2 < 70 mmHg or A-a gradient >= 35; alternatives include pentamidine, atovaquone, or primaquine with clindamycin.
prevention: TMP-SMX prophylaxis when CD4 < 200, and in many transplant and chemotherapy patients.
pearls: Ergosterol absent, so azoles and amphotericin B do not work
Steroids for hypoxic patients

name: Histoplasma capsulatum
structure: Dimorphic: mold in the environment, small yeast inside macrophages at body temperature.
genome: Haploid genome of about 30-40 Mb.
transmission: Inhalation of spores from soil with bird or bat droppings (caves, chicken coops); endemic to the Mississippi and Ohio River valleys and parts of Latin America, Africa and Asia.
diseases: Usually asymptomatic or self-limited pneumonia
Chronic cavitary histoplasmosis
Disseminated histoplasmosis in immunocompromised hosts: hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, oral ulcers, adrenal insufficiency
virulence: Survives and replicates inside macrophages
diagnosis: Urine and serum antigen; culture; histology showing intracellular yeast in macrophages.
treatment: Itraconazole for mild to moderate disease; liposomal amphotericin B for severe or disseminated disease.
prevention: Avoid exposure in high-risk activities; masks.
pearls: Bird and bat droppings; caves
Yeasts inside macrophages

name: Plasmodium falciparum
structure: Intracellular protozoan; in blood films shows multiple ring forms per red cell, appliqué forms and banana (crescent) shaped gametocytes.
genome: 14 chromosomes (about 23 Mb), very AT rich.
transmission: Bite of a female Anopheles mosquito (sporozoites); also transfusion and congenital.
diseases: Malaria: cyclic fevers, chills, anemia, splenomegaly
Severe malaria: cerebral malaria, severe anemia, hypoglycemia, acute kidney injury (blackwater fever), ARDS
virulence: PfEMP1 on infected red cells causes cytoadherence and sequestration in small vessels (brain, placenta)
No dormant liver stage (unlike P. vivax and P. ovale)
diagnosis: Thick and thin blood smears (Giemsa) repeated every 12-24 hours; rapid diagnostic antigen tests (HRP2); PCR.
treatment: Uncomplicated: artemisinin-based combination therapy (e.g., artemether-lumefantrine) or atovaquone-proguanil; chloroquine only in the few sensitive regions. Severe: IV artesunate.
prevention: Insecticide-treated nets, indoor spraying; chemoprophylaxis for travelers (atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine); RTS,S and R21 vaccines for children in endemic areas.
pearls: Sickle cell trait, G6PD deficiency and thalassemia offer some protection
Test G6PD before primaquine or tafenoquine (used for P. vivax/ovale hypnozoites)

name: Toxoplasma gondii
structure: Obligate intracellular crescent-shaped tachyzoites; tissue cysts containing bradyzoites persist in brain and muscle.
genome: Haploid genome of about 65 Mb.
transmission: Ingestion of oocysts in cat feces or tissue cysts in undercooked meat; transplacental.
diseases: Usually asymptomatic or a mononucleosis-like illness
Congenital toxoplasmosis: chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, diffuse intracranial calcifications
Toxoplasmic encephalitis in AIDS (CD4 < 100): multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions
Chorioretinitis
virulence: Intracellular replication within a parasitophorous vacuole; lifelong cysts
diagnosis: Serology (IgG, IgM, avidity); PCR of amniotic fluid; brain imaging with response to therapy in HIV.
treatment: Pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine plus leucovorin; spiramycin in early pregnancy to reduce transmission.
prevention: TMP-SMX prophylaxis when CD4 < 100 and Toxoplasma IgG positive; pregnant people avoid cat litter and undercooked meat.
pearls: Ring-enhancing lesions in HIV: toxoplasmosis vs primary CNS lymphoma (single lesion, EBV positive)
Leucovorin prevents pyrimethamine-induced folate deficiency

name: Giardia duodenalis (lamblia)
structure: Pear-shaped binucleate trophozoite with a ventral sucking disk and four pairs of flagella ('falling leaf' motility); infective cysts.
genome: Two nuclei, each tetraploid; genome of about 12 Mb.
transmission: Ingestion of cysts in contaminated water (campers, travelers), person to person (day care), and sexual (oral-anal).
diseases: Giardiasis: foul-smelling, fatty, non-bloody diarrhea, bloating, flatulence, weight loss; may cause lactose intolerance
virulence: Adheres to duodenal epithelium with the ventral disk, causing malabsorption
Severe or chronic in IgA deficiency and X-linked agammaglobulinemia
diagnosis: Stool antigen test or multiplex PCR; trophozoites or cysts in stool.
treatment: Tinidazole, nitazoxanide or metronidazole.
prevention: Boiling or filtering water; hand hygiene.
pearls: Fatty diarrhea after drinking stream water
Recurrent giardiasis: consider IgA deficiency

name: Entamoeba histolytica
structure: Amoeboid trophozoites that ingest red blood cells; cysts with up to four nuclei.
genome: Genome of about 20 Mb.
transmission: Fecal-oral ingestion of cysts in contaminated food or water.
diseases: Amebic dysentery: bloody diarrhea with flask-shaped colonic ulcers
Amebic liver abscess ('anchovy paste' pus), usually in the right lobe
virulence: Gal/GalNAc lectin for adherence, amebapores and cysteine proteases for tissue invasion
diagnosis: Stool antigen or PCR; serology for liver abscess; trophozoites with ingested RBCs on microscopy.
treatment: Metronidazole or tinidazole for invasive disease, followed by a luminal agent (paromomycin or iodoquinol) to clear cysts.
prevention: Safe water and sanitation.
pearls: Flask-shaped ulcers
Always follow tissue therapy with a luminal agent

name: Trypanosoma cruzi
structure: Flagellated trypomastigotes in blood; intracellular amastigotes in cardiac and smooth muscle.
genome: Diploid genome of about 55 Mb; kinetoplast DNA.
transmission: Feces of the reduviid (triatomine, 'kissing') bug rubbed into the bite wound or mucosa; also transfusion, congenital and oral (contaminated food). Endemic in Latin America.
diseases: Acute Chagas disease: fever, Romana sign (unilateral periorbital swelling), chagoma
Chronic Chagas: dilated cardiomyopathy with apical aneurysm, right bundle branch block, arrhythmias; megaesophagus and megacolon
virulence: Destroys myenteric plexus neurons and cardiac myocytes
diagnosis: Acute: blood smear or PCR. Chronic: two different serologic tests.
treatment: Benznidazole or nifurtimox (most effective in acute and early chronic disease).
prevention: Vector control, blood donor screening, screening in pregnancy.
pearls: Achalasia-like megaesophagus with heart failure in a Latin American patient

name: Leishmania donovani
structure: Promastigotes in the sandfly; non-flagellated amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies) inside macrophages.
genome: Genome of about 32 Mb in 36 chromosomes.
transmission: Bite of a female sandfly (Phlebotomus or Lutzomyia).
diseases: Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar): fever, massive splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, pancytopenia, weight loss, skin darkening
Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis
Other species cause cutaneous ulcers (L. major, L. tropica, common in Pakistan) and mucocutaneous disease (L. braziliensis)
virulence: Survives within macrophage phagolysosomes
diagnosis: Amastigotes in splenic, bone marrow or lymph node aspirates; rK39 rapid antigen test; PCR.
treatment: Liposomal amphotericin B; alternatives include miltefosine, pentavalent antimonials (sodium stibogluconate) and paromomycin depending on region.
prevention: Sandfly control, bed nets.
pearls: Massive splenomegaly with pancytopenia and fever
Cutaneous leishmaniasis is common in Pakistan and Afghanistan

name: Schistosoma species
structure: Separate-sex flukes living in venous plexuses; eggs with distinctive spines (S. mansoni lateral spine, S. haematobium terminal spine).
genome: Diploid genome of about 360-400 Mb.
transmission: Cercariae released from freshwater snails penetrate the skin during contact with fresh water.
diseases: Swimmer's itch and acute schistosomiasis (Katayama fever)
S. mansoni and S. japonicum: periportal 'pipestem' fibrosis, portal hypertension, splenomegaly
S. haematobium: hematuria, bladder fibrosis, squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder
virulence: Granulomatous reaction to trapped eggs causes fibrosis
diagnosis: Eggs in stool or urine; serology.
treatment: Praziquantel.
prevention: Avoid fresh water contact in endemic areas; mass drug administration; snail control.
pearls: S. haematobium and squamous cell bladder cancer
Praziquantel for flukes and tapeworms
